title: Sambo: self-defence without weapons
text: To a foreign visitor, the sight of two fighters in red and blue jackets may look like a variation of judo. In fact, the two sports share an ancestor but differ in important ways. Sambo, whose name comes from the Russian words for 'self-defence without weapons', was developed in the Soviet Union in the 1920s and 1930s, and today it is practised on every continent. Visitors are often surprised by how quickly the action moves: a fight lasts only a few minutes, and most of it is spent standing up, in a constant struggle for balance and grip.

Its creators worked independently at first, and it took years to combine their ideas into one set of rules. They wanted a system that would be useful for soldiers and police officers but also attractive as a sport. One of them, Vasily Oshchepkov, had studied judo in Japan, while another, Anatoly Kharlampiev, collected wrestling techniques from different regions of the country. The result combined throws and holds from judo with local traditions in a form that was easy to learn. Leg locks, which are not allowed in judo competitions, were included, too. At first the system was taught mainly in the army and the police, but it soon spread to sports clubs and schools, where thousands of young people began to train.

After the Second World War, the sport spread slowly beyond the borders of the USSR. Its first international events were held in Europe, and in the 1980s an international federation was established to organise championships. Early on, sambo had to compete for attention with better-known martial arts, but its reputation grew through the success of its athletes, some of whom later became famous in mixed martial arts. Because the sport borrowed from so many traditions, it offered an unusual variety of techniques. Coaches from other countries found this both interesting and difficult to learn.

Two main forms exist today. Sport sambo is the more familiar version: fighters win by throws, holds and painful locks, and strikes are not permitted. Combat sambo is much tougher, with punches and kicks, and the participants wear protective equipment. Both versions require physical strength, but coaches insist that quick thinking is just as important, since a bout can change in a moment. Points are awarded for clean throws and holds, and a perfect throw can end the fight at once. Women compete in both forms, in separate weight categories.

For young people, the appeal is practical. Training teaches how to fall without injury, and many beginners say it makes them feel more self-assured in everyday life. Teenagers who train regularly often find that their balance and reaction speed improve, which helps in other sports as well. Many clubs also run separate groups for children, where the emphasis is on games and safe falling rather than on competition. Classes are often cheaper than in other sports, because little equipment is needed. Coaches warn, however, that sambo is not a quick route to confidence: the first months are usually difficult, and most beginners spend a lot of time simply learning to fall.

Whether sambo will ever become an Olympic sport remains an open question. Supporters argue that its wide popularity and attractive style deserve a place at the Games. Critics point out that the number of Olympic events is limited and that other martial arts have a longer international history. Meanwhile, the sport continues to grow, quietly but steadily, in clubs and schools from Brazil to Mongolia. Many clubs also organise open lessons for beginners, hoping that curiosity will bring new members through the door. Whatever happens, sambo already has something many sports lack: a loyal community of fighters who consider it entirely their own.

questions.q: What does the text suggest about sambo and judo?
options: They are practised by the same athletes.
They have a common origin but are different.
They were invented by the same person.
They use identical rules in competitions.

options: The slow spread of the sport abroad.
Rivalry with more famous fighting sports.
The later careers of some athletes in other combat disciplines.
The variety of techniques taken from many traditions.
